## Reference-entry detection, fired on the anthology

*2026-10-01 02:00:04*

**The forcing function had been answered by the bibliography.** The anthology
opted ten fields into `explain: cited`. Asked whether that was making its
prose richer, the measurement said no. About half of the 1427 explained
relations were satisfied by a document's own reference line, `Author (Year),
LIT-nnn — ARXIV-…`, which names the paper and says nothing about it. The
check only bit on the 81 relations whose code appeared nowhere at all.

**The detector reads shape, because the heading is one record's habit.** The
first idea was to skip `## Source`. That fails on every record that names the
section differently, and it would skip annotated entries filed under it.
`luria/bibliography.py` judges each paragraph or list item on its own, by
four signals:
- an author lead that ends at a year, or a classic list of initials and
  surnames;
- identifiers;
- a title, dropped only when a venue or an identifier follows it;
- how much prose is left over.

**What separated entries from prose was case, not connectives.** The first
version asked for two function words among six leftover words. On the
anthology it hid "Two groups, three months apart, the same bug and two
different fixes." and "Two groups, two corpora, two instruments, no citation
in either direction." Both are annotations, terse enough to have almost no
connectives. Counting lower-case words fixed both. Names, initials and
acronyms are capitalised, so authors surviving from a second entry on the
line no longer count as prose either. Now eight lower-case words, or five
with two connectives, read as prose.

**Missed shapes found on the real corpus, each now a test:**
- an affiliation after `et al.` (`Shi et al., Meta (2023)`);
- a lower-case corporate author (`The Movie Gen team (2024)`);
- affiliations containing `of` and `at` (`University of Texas at Austin`);
- `and colleagues`.

The classic formats (APA, numbered, markdown link lists) were never seen on
the anthology, and are in the tests on their own merit.

**Fired on the anthology with the ten fields as configured: 590
findings**, all of them "cites X only in a reference entry (line n)":
- `SOTA.source` 267;
- `SOTA.introduced_by` 253;
- `THEORY.source` 70.

Every other explained field was already discussed in prose. Two checks of
the result:
- **The line-based count disagreed on 133.** Sampled, they are explanations
  that wrap onto the next line, or annotated entries. The block-level
  judgement is right about them.
- **38 of the 590 discuss the paper by its first author's name without the
  code** ("…Hoffmann et al."). That is still a finding worth having: the fix
  is to write the code in that sentence, which the anthology's own linking
  rule asks for anyway.

## A vocabulary is a scheme in shorthand

*2026-10-01 18:30:16*

**The question was hierarchy.** [#298](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/298) proposed union vocabularies, and behind
it sat a bigger ask: can a record express a hierarchical ontology? A sweep of
the code, the decisions, the docs and the issues found nothing. `groups:` is
a single level, a group is not a value anyone can tag with, and nothing rolls
up. A union would have added composition (one field accepting a cat or a
dog) but not subsumption: "cat" would still not be a term.

**The experiment that settled it used records, not config.** A `TERM`
scheme with a `broader`/`narrower` converse, a chain over `broader`, and
notes citing terms through a reference rendered Pet → Cat → {Tabby, Calico}
as a tree. It refused a citation of a term that did not exist, and gave
every term a status. So the hierarchy was already expressible; what the
record lacked was the move from vocabulary to scheme. The owner's reading:
a vocabulary is a tiny constrained scheme, and a record that wants more from
one is showing a type error, so the mechanism to build is promotion, not a
richer vocabulary ([ADR-124](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-124.md)).

**The trap was the views.** Hand-converting a vocabulary in a scratch
record linted clean and silently lost two things:

- **Index grouping.** The index could group only by a `fields:` entry, and
  `axis` refused a reference. Nothing listed which RFCs were in an area any
  more, except the published site's backlinks.
- **The old pages.** `docs/rfcs/area/runtime.md` was left behind. The
  directory stopped being one the generator owns once the field stopped
  being grouped, so `luria index` neither rewrote nor removed it, and
  nothing reported it.

The first is now `group: true` on a reference (and `axis` may name one), so
promotion keeps its views. Promotion keeps the field grouped, which makes
the second a non-issue for promotion. It remains a gap for any field that
stops being grouped by hand.

A converse listing each term's members was the cheaper alternative, and was
rejected. It needs no index change, but it makes every tagged document edit
its term's file, which turns popular terms into merge hot spots ([DP-2](../../record/principles.d/DP-002.md)).

**Things found on the way:**

- **The migration scaffold was still TOML.** `luria new migration` wrote
  `title = "…"` into a `.yaml` file that `luria migrate` reads with
  `yaml.safe_load`, where it parsed as one string. A test pinned the TOML
  spelling, so the suite had been enforcing the bug. The scaffold is YAML
  now, and a test parses its commented examples into operations the
  planner knows.
- **A dry run swept for nothing.** It walked every tracked file even when
  the plan had no code renames, which also made it need git. It now skips
  the walk unless there is something to sweep.
- **`modeling.md` still pointed at `statuses.yaml`.** Its "smells" section
  named the file — another stale mention of it, found after
  the second review. Grepping for the vocabulary of a stale claim is what
  finds them, and reading the flagged line is not.
- **The decision-shaped template leaked into promoted terms.** With no
  `_template.md`, `new_scheme_doc` falls back to a form that seeds
  `tags: [record]` and "Why this needed deciding" prose. Promotion now
  writes the scheme's template and stub the way `luria init` does, drops
  the seeded `tags`, and uses the value's blurb (or a provenance line) as
  the body.

**Then the numbers.** Promotion first rewrote `area: [runtime]` to
`area: [AREA-001]`: typed, checked, and unreadable. Derived aliases
already existed ([ADR-088](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-088.md)). A scheme's `alias: "AREA-{slug}"` makes
`AREA-runtime` resolve to AREA-001, and the fixer keeps it. But only prose
honoured them: a reference field rejected `AREA-runtime` as "not a code",
and so did `luria relate`. Every reader of a reference value had its own
resolution:
- the contract;
- the typed edges;
- two copies of `_codes` in chains and relations;
- invariants' `held`;
- the grouping;
- `relate`.

They now share one, `aliases.derived_code`. The converse fixer writes the
alias spelling too, and drops either spelling, because a removal by code
alone would have silently missed an alias.

The alias is derived from the slug, not the title. A title is a label: it
has spaces and capitals, and can differ from the value entirely. The slug
*is* the old value, so documents keep reading as they did. An alias tail
allows only letters, digits, dots and hyphens, so `long_term` slugs to
`long-term`. Two values slugging alike, or one that would read as a number
(`AREA-7` is a code, and a code outranks an alias), are refused.

Linting this repository took the same time with alias resolution on the
reference path (5.6s against 5.4s on `main`). The alias map is cached per
config, and the lookup runs only when some scheme declares an alias.

## A fresh record should have nothing to say

*2026-10-02 05:52:56*

**[#331](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/331), and why the existing guard missed it.**
`test_a_fresh_default_init_lints_clean` runs `init`, `index` and `lint`. But
`lint.run()` only raises on violations, so warnings passed it, and three of
them printed on every new record. The new test (`tests/test_fresh_init.py`)
captures what `lint` prints and requires nothing but the all-clear. It covers
the default config and a custom one with no principles scheme, which is the
shape the RFC tutorial uses.

**CLAUDE.md was a copy, not a plan.** `docs/README.md` has been planned from
the config since [ADR-048](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-048.md). `CLAUDE.md` was copied verbatim, and its first
paragraph links `docs/design-principles.md`. In a record with no principles
scheme that link points at a page nothing will ever generate, and
`broken-targets` said so on day one. The paragraph now follows the config.
It points where a document-rendered scheme writes `paths.design_principles`,
and is left out when no scheme does. The broken links seen *before* the
first `luria index` are a different matter: those pages are generated, and
`init` already says to index before linting, so that state is expected.

**`spent-upgrades` was talking to the wrong reader.** Its own devlog entry
(2026-09-06) describes it firing on luria's record "the moment its own
upgrade ran, which is the guard working". The remedy it names, "remove it at
1.0.0", is a change to luria. A downstream record can't make that change. A
record born on YAML never needed the upgrade at all, so for its owner the
row could only teach them to skim past a finding.

Two narrower fixes didn't hold up:
- **Look at git history** for a `luria.toml` the record once had. Both this
  checkout and CI's are shallow, so the answer would depend on clone depth.
- **Have `init` write a `mute` line.** `init` never overwrites a
  `luria.yaml`, so the tutorial path, where the config is written first,
  wouldn't get it.

What does hold is scoping by who can act. The finding is reported only when
the running `luria/upgrade.py` lives inside the record's root, which is true
for luria's own checkout because CI installs it editable (`pip-spec: -e .`).
Along the way: `spent_upgrades()` runs one plan (the statuses one) for every
entry in `SUNSET`, so the `yaml` row has never been checked on its own. That
is unchanged here.

**`collect` crashed on the directory `init` had just made.** The default
`record/changelog.d` has a target, `CHANGELOG.md`, that nothing wrote.
`init` now writes each fragment directory's target with a heading and the
insert marker. `collect` still refuses to create a missing target itself:
what goes above the marker is a choice about the file. But the refusal is
now a message that names the file and says `luria init` writes it, instead
of a `FileNotFoundError`.

## A catch-all keyword swallows --help

*2026-10-02 12:48:14*

**[#328](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/328).** `luria new --help` answered "no such field 'help'". Fire shows a
function's help when it sees `--help` only if the function has no
`**kwargs` to hand it to. `new.run` has one: it accepts a scheme's declared
fields as flags (`--source LIT-134` where SOTA declares `source`). So
`--help` arrived as `declared={'help': True}` and was refused like any
undeclared field. Any other command that grows a catch-all will do the same.

The fix pops `help`/`h` before field parsing, and prints the one thing the
generic Fire help never could: the kinds this record scaffolds and the flags
each takes, read from `luria.yaml` like the dispatch ([ADR-036](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-036.md)). Those are
what a first-time reader gets wrong. The first docs draft wrote
`luria new RFC` four times, when kinds are the lowercased prefix. One
per-kind flag list (`accepted_flags`) now feeds both help and the refusal
message. The refusal had been listing a scheme's declared `status` and
`tags` twice, once as universal flags and once as declared fields.

Not done here: a fragment or journal still accepts flags it ignores
(`luria new changelog --title`, [#330](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/330)). `accepted_flags` is the list a
refusal would read.

## Duplicate keys: ask the parser

*2026-10-02 15:26:26*

**[#240](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/240).** The duplicate-key half of `frontmatter_shape` compared the raw text before the first colon, on unindented lines only. That approximates YAML without being YAML: `"title":` after `title:`, and any repeated key in a nested mapping, both collapsed silently. That is the [#164](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/164) defect again in other spellings. The check now loads the block with a `SafeLoader` subclass that refuses a repeated key in any mapping, so the parser that does the collapsing is the one asked. The `<!--` half stays a text check, because no loader raises on a key that happens to read `<!--`.

Two details the issue's sketch did not cover:
- **`<<` merge keys** are skipped. An explicit key after a merge is how YAML spells an override.
- **The line number** comes free from the key node's mark, so the finding names it. The issue had expected to lose it.

**Journals were never checked.** `check_journals` parsed frontmatter but never called the shape check, so a devlog entry could pass the lint and still fail the Pages build. It now runs the same check, and still reads its metadata through the cached `read_document`.

**Fired once on a real case.** The issue's repro (`"title": dup` above `title:` in [ADR-124](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-124.md)) and a nested duplicate in a real devlog entry were both reported with the right lines, then reverted. This record lints clean under the stricter check. Lint time: 5.8s against 5.4s on `main`, using the C loader where it is built.

## Forbidding a field: the mirror of required_when

*2026-10-02 16:25:50*

**[#191](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/191) was still open after a month of features.** Before building, I checked whether anything since could express it. `excluded_by` (now on any field since [ADR-098](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-098.md)) compares values within one field. `field_groups` counts present fields, and `status` is always present. Derived fields have no conditionals. The issue's exact case still linted clean on `main`. So `forbidden_when` takes `required_when`'s condition in the opposite sense ([ADR-125](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-125.md)). The built-in successor field forbids itself while `status` is the scheme's `active` word.

**One condition, two keys.** `_when` parses the shape for both keys, and `_conditions` yields both to the same load-time check, so a misspelled field or value fails for either. Contradictions are refused at load: required and forbidden, a value in both lists, and forbidden on a field with a `default`. The last is easy to miss. A default is never absent, so the rule would fire on documents that never wrote the field.

**Three existing tests were standing in the forbidden state.** Two contract tests and an annotation test put `superseded_by` on an `Active` fixture, because nothing had ever said that was wrong. They were about remote resolution and the annotation fixer, not status, so their fixtures now retire the document first.

**The annotation fixer refused on its own.** `annotations` already declines a write that would leave a document in breach of its contract. A `ref::superseded_by:` annotation on an `Active` note is now reported as a bad annotation instead of being written. No new code was needed for that, and a test now pins it.

**Fired once on a real case.** In a scratch record from `luria init`, [ADR-001](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-001.md) at `Active` with `superseded_by: [ADR-002]` printed `luria: docs lint clean` on `main`. On this branch it is a violation naming `status: Active` and the ADR. This record and every example lint clean under the rule, so none of them held the contradiction.

**Not mine:** `ADR-122.md:123: ref::extended_by names no reference field` prints on `main` too.

## Title comparison folds spelling, not meaning

*2026-10-02 19:38:00*

**[#340](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/340).** arXiv began returning a title in TeX (`$O(n^2)$`), and `normalize()` read it as a different title from the recorded `O(n²)`. The `²` was dropped outright, while `^2` kept its digit behind a separator. Accented letters were also dropped outright. `normalize()` now folds spelling before comparing: it unwraps TeX, applies Unicode NFKD and drops combining marks, names Greek letters (`µ` → `μ` → `mu`, meeting `\mu`), and compares with every separator removed.

**The order of the TeX passes matters.**
1. Formatting commands (`\textbf`, `\mathcal`, …) go first and keep their argument.
2. Letter accents (`\v{c}`) go next. They count as accents only when followed by `{`, so `\cite` and `\boldsymbol` aren't eaten.
3. Then symbol accents and escaped punctuation (`\"o`, `\&`).
4. Only then do remaining control words become their names.

`\varepsilon`, `ε` and `ϵ` all reach `epsilon`, since the variant glyph is the same letter.

**What it must not fold** is pinned in tests: `\mu` vs `\nu`, `n^2` vs `n^3`, and the AdamW nickname. The accepted cost is that `data set` equals `dataset`. For "is this the same paper" that is wanted.

**Not checked on the real case.** `LIT-655` lives in anthology-of-the-sota, which this session can't reach. The issue's own acceptance step covers it: after release, its `source-ok:` should be reported as excusing nothing. No `source-ok:` in this repository or its examples flips.

## A typed number: on a temporary document became a duplicate key on the trunk

*2026-10-03 20:51:18*

The anthology's lint failed on its own `main`, in
`record/decisions.d/ADR-066.md`: a duplicate frontmatter key, `number`. The
bot's concretize commit (anthology 743847cd) had written `number: 66` *above*
an existing `number: tmptzokf`, and nothing in the PR that filed
ADR-tmptzokf had complained.

## Why it happened

`luria new` leaves `number:` out of a merge-allocated document, so concretize
normally has nothing to replace. This document had been written by hand, and
its author typed `number: tmptzokf`. `write_number` was meant to replace an
existing line; its docstring says so, and
`test_write_number_replaces_rather_than_duplicates` tests it. But
`_NUMBER_LINE` matched only `\d*`, the shape the writers themselves produce.
A non-numeric value fell through to the insert branch.

The first theory was that concretize had a separate insertion path for
renamed files. It does not. `concretize.run` calls the same
`new.write_number` that `luria repair` uses, so `repair` had the same gap: a
numbered document carrying a malformed `number:` would also have gained a
second key. One pattern fix covers both callers.

## Why the lint had not caught it earlier

`check_numbers` skips temporary documents outright, reasonably, since they
have no number to compare with the filename. So a typed `number:` on a temp
document passed every check on the branch. It became a violation only once
concretize ran on the trunk, which nobody reviews. That is the wrong place for
a defect to surface. The check now reports it on the branch, and `luria
repair` removes the line.

## Fired on a real case

With the fix installed, `luria lint` on the anthology at 987ae08f, the commit
that filed ADR-tmptzokf, reports
`ADR-tmptzokf.md: a temporary document declares number:`. `luria repair` then
removes the line, leaving `status:` first in the frontmatter.

## Multi-scheme references: fired on the constitution example

*2026-10-07 00:37:39*

[#160](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/160) asked for `scheme:` to take a list. The change is the decision in
[ADR-126](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-126.md); this entry records how it was checked and what turned up along
the way.

**Fired before trusting.** On a scratch copy of `examples/constitution`,
`BOUNDARY-003` was given `overrides: [PRACTICE-010, BOUNDARY-001]`:

- With the shipped `scheme: PRACTICE`, the lint reported `overrides:
  BOUNDARY-001 is not a PRACTICE code`. That is the failure [#160](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/160) described,
  reproduced.
- With `scheme: [PRACTICE, BOUNDARY]`, the lint exited 0.
- With the edge changed to `VALUE-001`, the lint reported `is not a PRACTICE
  or BOUNDARY code — a BOUNDARY document's overrides names a PRACTICE or
  BOUNDARY document`. The union is checked, not just widened.

None of the example's three boundaries actually overrides another, so the
committed example widens the declaration and leaves the documents alone.
Inventing an edge to show the feature off would have put a false claim in a
worked record.

**Where single-scheme assumptions lived.** The sites that read a reference's
target were found by grepping `.scheme`, `.reference` and `ANY_SCHEME`,
not by following failures, because several would have kept passing while
quietly wrong:

- `code.startswith(f"{target}-")` with a tuple target formats as
  `('LIT',)-` and silently matches nothing. It raises no error.
- `field.reference == ANY_SCHEME` against an unconverted string sentinel
  would have stayed False for every field.
- `converse_scheme_of` would have answered with the first target only.

`ANY_SCHEME` became `("*",)` alongside the change, so every comparison is
tuple against tuple. Every consumer goes through `contract.targets`,
`target_of` and `spelled`.

**The converse decomposed cleanly.** `relations.pairs()` now yields one pair
per target scheme. The crossing-pair machinery from [ADR-097](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-097.md) already filtered
each side's reading to the far scheme's documents, so a multi-scheme field
split into independent per-target pairs and the fixer needed no other change.
`edges()` was the one reader that took a single far scheme. It now unions
the far documents and reads the converse back from each target.

**Two test mistakes worth not repeating.** `_config.merged` deep-merges, so
removing a key from the *extra* fragment leaves the base's copy in place. A
test that wants a key gone has to write the whole config. And a converse
that names a third scheme makes that scheme owe the far field. That is the
rule working, not a bug, though it read like one at first.

## The facts layer, and three assumptions it corrected

*2026-10-07 04:29:47*

The first step of the logic-core migration: `luria/facts.py` reads the
configuration and every document into ground atoms, `luria/logic/` runs
clingo programs over them, and `tools/parity.py` holds every later step to
byte-identical `luria lint` and `luria index` output against the last
release.

**The harness was fired twice before being trusted.** Run against itself,
0.36.0 was byte-identical on all ten records: luria's own, nucleation, the
anthology and the seven examples, about seven minutes in all. That shows
the comparison is deterministic. A one-word sabotage of the chain renderer
then produced three reported differences on the anthology, each with a
unified diff. Two things make it hermetic: `lint.network: never` in each
copy, so arXiv being slow or throttling cannot move the output, and copying
the `.git` with each record, because the converse fixer reads HEAD.

**Three assumptions the tests corrected.** Each is worth knowing before
writing rules against these facts:

- **An unpadded code is not an alias.** `LIT-1` does not resolve to
  `LIT-001`: `codes_of` resolves derived aliases, not numbering. The facts
  report what luria reads, so `ref_value` holds `LIT-1`.
- **`edge/3` is not "edges that land".** `edges.graph` keeps any code of a
  declared scheme, resolved or not. Whether a target exists is `doc/2`'s
  business, and a rule that needs landing must join on it.
- **clingo stops at the first model by default.** The wrapper refuses a
  program with more than one answer set, because a generated view must be a
  function of its sources. With `--models=1` it could never see a second
  answer set, so the guard passed a program with four. It now asks for two.

**Scale.** The anthology is 39,385 facts, extracted in 1.6 seconds: 29,439
`value`, 3,144 `edge`, 3,126 `ref_value`, 1,769 documents.

<a id="20261007045624"></a>

## Logic core step 2: invariants, and what parity had to cover

*2026-10-07 04:56:24*

The second step of the logic-core migration moves the invariant check and
the reading every chain walk starts from (`relations.edges`) to clingo.
`relations.lp` derives `held/4`, a relation read from both sides;
`invariants.lp` derives unbound relation pairs, unbound chain edges, and
components with no common value, taking each component's least code as its
name with `#min`. Python keeps the wording and the order.

**The order was the part to get right, not the logic.** The report prints
findings in the order the old walks produced them, and `findings()`
deduplicates by first appearance, relations before chains. Chain pairs and
lines come out sorted, so `sorted()` reproduces them. A relation pair is met
first at whichever of its two directed readings sorts lower among those the
near side actually holds, so that is the sort key. Without it, a cross-scheme
pair whose near document sorts after its far one would move.

**Parity now runs `luria reports` too.** The invariant findings reach a
user through `docs/reports/unbound-lineage.md`, which `luria index` does not
write, so the step-1 harness could not have seen a regression here. 0.36.0
against itself is still byte-identical with the step added.

**Fired on real cases.** The anthology declares a cross-scheme relation
invariant (`SOTA.source`) and three chain invariants, and has two unbound
lines, one of 140 members. All ten records are byte-identical to 0.36.0
across lint, index and reports. Anthology lint went from about 71 s to
about 68 s. The facts are memoised against the config and a stat
fingerprint of the documents, so a fixer that writes between questions is
read again.

`holds/3` comes from `facts.members`, and `invariants.held` now calls it too,
so the rules and the shell compare the same sets by construction.

<a id="20261007054401"></a>

## Logic core step 3: the converse fixer, and a harness that gives it work

*2026-10-07 05:44:01*

Step 3 of the logic-core migration moves the converse decisions to
`luria/logic/converse.lp`. Each pair is `(S, F, B, T)`. From the working
tree and from HEAD it derives the two sides of every edge. It then
classifies each edge by what changed: written to both sides, taken from
both, or a clash. A clash is either a directed relation asserted both ways
or a withdrawal on one side against an assertion on the other. The HEAD
baseline is a new fact, `head_value/4`, read by one `git grep` per scheme
instead of one per pair and side. The commit HEAD names joins the facts'
fingerprint, so a commit between two questions in one process is seen.

**[#358](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/358) falls out.** The Python kept a pair's two sides in a dict keyed by
field name, so a symmetric relation crossing schemes collided with itself.
The rules name the sides `now_f` and `now_b`, so there is nothing to collide.
[#358](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/358)'s three regression tests are carried into this branch. They fail
against the old Python and pass against the rules, with none of [#358](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/358)'s
patch applied.

**Parity had to be given something to check.** On a record whose relations
already agree, the fixer has no work, so byte parity on lint, index and
reports says almost nothing about it. The harness now also runs
`luria link` and `luria link --fix`. With `--perturb SEED` it first drops
one paired code from a seeded third of the eligible documents and commits
that, then drops one from another third and leaves it uncommitted. The
first third is untouched one-sided edges, which the fixer completes. The
second is withdrawals, which it propagates. It was fired first with 0.36.0
against itself. On nucleation, 206 documents were perturbed and `luria
link` proposed 67 writes and 54 removals in 111 files, byte-identical
between two runs.

<a id="20261007062418"></a>

## Logic core step 4: config consistency, and timing markers

*2026-10-07 06:24:18*

Step 4 moves the cross-scheme checks that `luria.yaml` must pass to
`luria/logic/consistency.lp`. They had been spread over `_checked_converse`,
`_check_invariants`, a loop in `_schemes` and the body of `_chains`. Each
refusal is now one derived atom. `luria/consistency.py` words it and raises
the least, using a key that reproduces the loader's old order: per scheme,
converses before invariants, and per chain the scheme, its facets, each
walked field, then output and invariant. So a config with several mistakes
still reports the same one first.

**Record parity cannot see this step.** A real record's config is valid
and never reaches a refusal. `tools/config_parity.py` therefore breaks one
in seeded ways and compares what each build raised, word for word. On
nucleation and the anthology, 700 mutants (300 mixed and 400 chain-only)
gave 583 refusals, all identical, and every refusal kind is represented.

**The tool was wrong the first time it ran.** `python -c` puts the working
directory on `sys.path`, so the "baseline" imported the checkout instead of
0.36.0, and every mutant "differed" by a missing `clingo` import. It runs
isolated (`-I`) now. After the fix, changing one word in one message was
caught: 13 of 60 chain mutants differed.

**Timing markers.** With `LURIA_TIMINGS=1`, luria prints the facts read, each
solve and the whole command to stderr. The parity harness prints per-step
seconds for both builds. The first use found something. On nucleation, inside
`luria lint`, the facts took 17.9 s of wall-clock time but 2.3 s when timed
alone (documents 1.3 s, HEAD baseline 1.1 s). The likely cause is the
render thread pool contending for the GIL while they are read, not the
reading itself. Each consistency solve takes 2 to 4 ms, and config load is
unchanged within noise.

<a id="20261007073403"></a>

## Why index and reports got slower, and the fix

*2026-10-07 07:34:03*

Step 4's timing table had the anthology's `luria index` at x1.20 and `luria
reports` at x1.40 against 0.36.0, from single runs. Three alternating runs
each confirmed it was real. `index` went from 20.0-20.8 s to 24.5-25.8 s and
`reports` from 15.6-16.2 s to 17.2-18.3 s.

`LURIA_TIMINGS` showed two separate causes.

**The facts were built twice.** Under the render pool, `index` built all
70,238 facts twice, taking 16.4 s and then 4.2 s. Serially (`LURIA_JOBS=1`) it
built them once in 3.0 s. Two threads asked at the same moment, both missed
the memo, and each built a copy, slowed by contending with the other. The
memo checked identity but nothing serialised the build. The facts and each
solve are now built under a lock, and a test has eight threads ask at once
and requires one build.

**Every command paid for every fact.** Timed alone, the HEAD baseline took
2.06 s, from one `git show` per file. `value` and `edge` (32k facts) are read
by no rule, and `holds` covered every field when the invariant rules only
ever read the fields an invariant names. Each `.lp` program now names the
families it reads in a `% facts:` line, and `derive` builds only those. For
`index` and `reports` that is 10,325 facts instead of 70,238. The baseline
reads through one `git cat-file --batch`. `luria facts` still prints every
family.

After the fix, over three alternating runs on the anthology:

- `index`: 0.36.0 took 19.7-20.8 s, the candidate 18.8-19.3 s.
- `reports`: 0.36.0 took 15.6-16.2 s, the candidate 13.7-14.9 s.
- `lint`: 0.36.0 took 74.8-83.4 s, the candidate 60.5-67.2 s.

**A caution about the markers.** `LURIA_TIMINGS` reports wall-clock time. A
solve that runs while the render pool holds the GIL can show 8 s for 0.2 s
of work. Per-phase lines say where time went in one run; whether a command
got slower is a question for the command totals over repeated runs.

<a id="20261007141754"></a>

## Logic core step 5: acknowledgements, and why contract stays in Python

*2026-10-07 14:17:54*

Step 5 was going to be the reference checks in `contract`. Reading them
first changed the plan. For each value they ask whether the code's prefix
is one the field names and whether the code is among that scheme's
documents. Those are two lookups, interleaved with parsing the value. And
`relations._blocked` asks the same checker about a document as it would read
after the fixer's edits, which exists only in memory. Record facts cannot
describe that without a solve per file. Rules there would read worse and run
slower, which are two of the ADR's kill criteria. The owner chose to drop
`contract` and port `ref_status` instead, and the ADR's list now says why.

What `ref_status` decides is a join: citation sites, annotations and
document states, matched by file, code, line and kind. The scan still finds
the sites in prose (blanking URLs, directives, `formerly:` entries, chain
fields and composed remote codes). It then hands
`luria/logic/acknowledgements.lp` the sites, the annotations and which codes
resolve and are in force. The program decides:

- **excused/2**: the first well-formed annotation in the file that names the
  code, governs the line and claims the site's state, and failing that the
  first `mention-ok`;
- **unused/1**: a well-formed annotation that answers for nothing;
- **lost/3**: what a malformed annotation left unacknowledged.

This replaces `mention_for`, the three `next(...)` excuse searches,
`Scan.used`'s identity walk over every site, and `_unexcused_under`.

On the anthology the scan finds 15,893 sites and 1,212 annotations. The
solve takes 0.3 s and the whole scan is unchanged: 0.36.0 took 7.4 s and
the candidate 6.9 s.

## The two timing follow-ups: a fixed cost, and wall time that was waiting

*2026-10-07 15:09:55*

Two questions were left open after the logic-core ports.

**The small examples were slower by a fixed amount.** Parity had them
0.1-0.3 s slower in total over five commands. Fifteen alternating runs per
command on `examples/knowledge-base` put the gap at +11 ms (`index`),
+23 ms (`reports`) and +32 ms (`lint`), as medians. The pieces:

- importing clingo, about 8 ms, which every command pays because config load
  checks consistency through it;
- about 1 ms per solve, mostly clingo parsing the rule text, with three at
  config load;
- `rules()` reading each `.lp` file on every call;
- one `git rev-parse` (about 1.5 ms) per read of the facts, to stamp HEAD.

Now rule files are cached, config load shares one answer between its two
scheme passes, and the HEAD stamp is the `HEAD` file plus `stat`s of the ref
it names and of `packed-refs`. git is asked for the git directory once per
root, and asked again if a `.git` appears. Re-measured, the gap is +12 to
+21 ms, within run-to-run noise of about 10 ms. The import is the floor, and
it is the price of the dependency.

**The facts took 17.9 s of wall time inside nucleation's lint.** That
figure predates the race fix; afterwards the facts took 0.28 s pooled
against 0.13 s serially. One phase still swelled: the first relations
solve, at 3.46 s pooled against 0.075 s serially. Taken apart serially, it is
9 ms building program text, 30 ms of clingo parsing, 7 ms grounding, 1 ms
solving and 12 ms converting. With the markers now reporting thread CPU time,
the pooled run says it directly: 3.918 s of wall time, 0.188 s of CPU. The
solve thread waited for the GIL behind the render pool, and the command
total is the same pooled or serial (about 55 s against 53 s). Nothing to fix
in the solve. The markers were what needed fixing, because a wall-time-only
line had invited exactly the misreading this follow-up was opened to check.

<a id="20261007180641"></a>

## Review fixes: one door for writes, a wheel smoke test, and git as optional

*2026-10-07 18:06:41*

A review of the logic-core stack raised three concerns. Fixing them turned
up a fourth problem.

**Stale reads after an in-process write.** The facts cache keyed on
`(path, mtime_ns, size)` and HEAD, and each solve keyed on the facts list's
identity. A same-size rewrite inside one tick of a coarse clock would leave
both stale. The review suggested a `facts.forget()` called from each
writer. The exposure turned out wider than the facts: they are built
through `adr_index.read_document`, whose parse cache has the same key, so
a rebuilt facts list would still read the old parse. The fix is one door.
`luria/writes.py` has `write_text` and `unlink`, and both call `wrote()`.
That drops the path's entries in the parse, number and listing caches. For
a scheme document it also bumps a generation that the facts are keyed on
(and through them every solve) and drops the reference scan. Generated
views do not bump it, so `luria index` does not rebuild the facts between
pages. An AST rewrite moved all 55 `write_text`/`unlink` calls in `luria/`
through it. `tests/test_writes.py` fails on any that comes back.

Two things the rewrite broke, which the suite caught:

- `upgrade.run` had a local list named `writes`, which shadowed the module.
- `wrote()` loaded the config to ask whether a path was a document, and
  `luria upgrade` must never load the config it repairs. It now asks only a
  config that is already loaded. With none loaded, nothing is cached
  against one, so it counts the write.

**The parity harness cannot see this**, because each command runs in a
fresh process. `test_a_rewrite_the_clock_misses_still_reaches_the_rules`
does: it derives, makes a same-size edit through the door, puts the old
mtime back with `os.utime`, and derives again. I sabotaged the generation
key and the parse-cache drop, and it failed as it should.

**Wheel coverage.** The tests run editable, so they read the `.lp` files
out of the checkout. `tools/wheel_smoke.py` takes the interpreter of a
clean environment the wheel was installed into. It checks that `luria`
imports from there, that every program in the source tree ships and loads
through `importlib.resources`, and that the installed CLI lints an example.
With `relations.lp` deleted from an installed copy, it reported
`the wheel lacks relations.lp`.

**The fourth problem: git had become a hard dependency.** The first smoke
run restricted `PATH` to the venv, and `luria lint` crashed with
`FileNotFoundError: git` in the new HEAD baseline code. 0.36.0 runs all of
lint, index, link --fix and reports without git. Every git call in
`facts.py` now goes through `_git`, which returns None when git cannot run,
and that reads as no repository. The smoke test runs the CLI with git and
without.

## Explicit relations: what the migration found, and the remote target it needed

*2026-10-08 04:48:39*

The request was to make configuration the only source of relation
semantics, so that the facts layer stops omitting relation types and
`relations.lp` stops inferring them from an absence. Three things came out
of doing it that were not in the request.

**Remote successors are real, so references can target remotes.** A scan of
every successor value in the ten records found one LIT in nucleation
superseded by an `ANTH-` code and one LIT in the anthology superseded by an
`ARXIV-` code. The implicit any-scheme reference had allowed these. A
concrete local target set could not, and an explicit `*` would have brought
back the thing being removed. So `scheme:` may now name declared remotes:
`scheme: [LIT, ARXIV]`. `contract.remotes_of` reads them, a remote code
passes where its remote is named, and the graph still draws no edge to a
remote.

**The index needed a role, not a rename.** The "shaped by" line read
`influenced_by` by name. Removing it would change the index pages of luria's
own record and the anthology. Keeping the name keeps the special case. So
`influence:` names the declared reference the index renders, as `successor`
does for retirement, and config load refuses one that names nothing
declared.

**The test helper was leaking.** `merged()` merged dict fragments by
reference, so one test's extra keys mutated a module-level fragment that
the next test reused. It only surfaced when the new tests passed role dicts
through it. It deep-copies now.

The migration reads the old config with its roles stripped in memory,
because an old config may name a `successor` it never declared. It does
this through `config.rooted(root, text=...)`, a new optional argument. It
loads the result before writing anything. On copies of the ten records it
inferred every target set by hand-checkable rule. Parity runs 0.36.0 on
the old record against the candidate on the migrated one, with
`tools/parity.py --upgrade explicit-relations`. One output differs by
design: `docs/record.md`, which now states each scheme's successor
obligation under that scheme instead of as a standard rule.

## Chains over path patterns: how the design got there, and what parses Cypher

*2026-10-13 02:56:00*

[#371](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/371) asks for chains over a derived relation, the follow-on [ADR-127](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-127.md)
left open. The draft decision, [ADR-129](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-129.md), went through three shapes
in one session, and the two that lost are worth not re-deriving.

**First: a field list on the scheme.** `composed: {leads_to: [premise_of,
concludes]}` covers claim → inference → claim and nothing else. It is a
path pattern with every feature removed, in a syntax of luria's own.

**Second: queries as clingo rule bodies.** [ADR-127](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-127.md)'s "user-facing queries"
read as user-written Datalog. That fails [ADR-125](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-125.md)'s "rule in the line". It
also lets a user recurse through negation, and takes away luria's ability
to check endpoints or name intermediates. The owner meant *path* queries,
and had suggested Cypher earlier for exactly this. [ADR-127](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-127.md) rejected Cypher
as an engine and praised its patterns, and those two are separable.

**The motivating case** that made path patterns the obvious notation: a
view walking a question through its answers, objections and replies to its
conclusion, as a unit a manuscript could later be composed from. Two
things came out of sketching it, both outside this ADR:

- That view is a tree across schemes, not a chain, so it needs an outline
  view kind.
- Argument acceptance with attack cycles is not stratified: a cycle gives
  several answer sets. It stays out of the pattern subset by keeping
  `WHERE NOT` off variable-length patterns.

**What exists for Cypher → Datalog, surveyed 2026-10-13:**

- **GraphGlot** (`graphglot` on PyPI, 0.14.3, Apache-2.0, pure Python,
  modelled on sqlglot). It parses GQL and Cypher to one AST and transpiles
  only between those, with no Datalog or SQL output. Fired on this ADR's
  patterns: the `neo4j` dialect parsed all of them, plus `*1..`, `{status:
  'Active'}` and `OPTIONAL MATCH`. The `fullgql` dialect rejects the Cypher
  spellings of variable length and negation, and accepts `->{1,}` and
  `NOT EXISTS { MATCH … }`. The AST is the full GQL program tree. The path
  sits under `GqlProgram → … → SimpleMatchStatement → GraphPattern →
  PathPatternList → PathTerm.factors`, which alternates `NodePattern` and
  `FullEdgePointingLeft`/`Right`. Pre-1.0, with releases days apart, so
  pin it.
- **Raqlet** (Shaikhha et al., CIDR 2026) compiles Cypher and SQL/PGQ to
  Datalog through two IRs. It is the real thing, but no public release
  turned up, and it targets Soufflé-style Datalog.
- **grand-cypher** executes a Cypher subset over networkx. Negated
  patterns and `OPTIONAL MATCH` are "help welcome", and it would be a
  second engine.
- **microsoft/openCypherTranspiler** targets T-SQL, and
  **cypher-for-gremlin** targets Gremlin. Neither fits.

So no tool translates Cypher to clingo for us, and luria writes the
lowering whatever parses. Given that, the owner chose a lark grammar of
luria's own over GraphGlot:

- GraphGlot's tree buries the path fifteen wrapper levels deep.
- It accepts all of Cypher, so the subset would need a second pass.
- It is a pre-1.0 dependency.

A scratch grammar was 15 rule lines:

```lark
// A path pattern: the subset ADR-129 admits.
start: path ("WHERE"i "NOT"i path)*

path: node (edge node)*

node: "(" VAR? (":" NAME)? props? ")"   // a bare (c) refers to a node bound earlier
props: "{" prop ("," prop)* "}"
prop: NAME ":" STRING

edge: "-[" VAR? types length? "]->"     -> right
    | "<-[" VAR? types length? "]-"     -> left
types: ":" NAME ("|" NAME)*
length: "*" INT? ".." INT?

VAR: /[a-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*/
NAME: /[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*/
STRING: /'[^']*'/ | /"[^"]*"/
%import common.INT
%import common.WS
%ignore WS
```

It parsed every pattern and refused
`OPTIONAL MATCH`, undirected edges and `RETURN`. Two gaps for the real one,
both closed in `luria/patterns.lark`: `*..3` now takes Cypher's default
lower bound of 1, and a bare `*` reads as `*1..`.

Its first run caught a rule the ADR had wrong. `WHERE NOT (c)<-…` names a
bound node without a label, so a node needs either a label or a back
reference. The trap for whoever builds it: lark's refusals are "unexpected
token at column N". So naming the out-of-subset construct (`RETURN`,
`OPTIONAL`, an undirected edge) is a check of its own, before or around
the parse.

## Building it

Three things the ADR got wrong or left out, found while implementing it:

- **Direction.** A chain nests the holder of a field under its target:
  `A extends B` puts A under B. A pattern stands in for a field, so its
  first node nests under its last. The ADR's first example,
  `leads_to: (a:CLAIM)-[:premise_of]->…->(b:CLAIM)`, would have hung
  premises under their conclusions. The example now reads backwards on
  purpose (`follows_from: (b)<-[:concludes]-(i)<-[:premise_of]-(a)`), and
  the config docstring says why.
- **A closure stays within one scheme.** Each step of `-[:f*]->` is
  `held/4` on the near node's scheme, so the documents between the ends
  have to be of that scheme too. That became a load-time refusal rather
  than a closure that silently stops after one step.
- **"also extends" ([#359](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/359)).** A step with two premises renders under one
  and names the other with the hard-coded "also extends". On a pattern
  chain that is wrong. [#359](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/359) names each extra parent by its relation and
  merged first. The conflict in `_load` and `_line_block` resolved by
  keeping both sides, and a pattern's name now reads in that place: "also
  follows from".

One trap from writing `examples/argument-map`: a document whose frontmatter
does not parse is all prose to `luria link --fix`, so the fixer wrote
markdown links into the frontmatter lines. The cause was a stray first line
from a shell `printf --`. The lint reported "no YAML frontmatter" first, but
by then the fixer had already run. Check that a new document parses before
running the fixer on it.

Fired on the example before trusting it. `docs/argument.md` shows each step
"through" its inference, and `docs/uncontested.md` drops the challenged
step. The example lints clean.

## Trying it on nucleation

Run on a scratch copy of dmarx/nucleation, with a worktree of `main` beside
the branch:

- **Parity holds.** Unchanged, all 625 files `luria index` writes are
  byte-identical between the two, and `luria lint` is too once
  `lint.network: never` is set in both copies. Run with the network on, the
  outputs differed only in which arXiv identifiers each run got throttled
  on, so compare with the network off.
- **The pattern earns its place.** `argued_from: (c:CLAIM)<-[:concludes]-
  (g:ARG)-[:rests_on]->(p:CLAIM)` on the `argument` chain draws the steps
  through ARG-006, ARG-007 and ARG-008, which a chain over `rests_on` never
  saw. ARG-004 is Rejected and drew a step too, until `WHERE NOT (g
  {status: 'Rejected'})` took it out. A bare back-reference with a property
  map does that, with no new syntax.
- **Built-in open ends failed, and were removed.** The first version listed
  every partial match that could not be completed under *Open* on the chain
  page. On nucleation it listed six arguments, all of them complete: they
  rest only on `grounds`, which nucleation's `premises` field group allows.
  It ignored `WHERE NOT`, so Rejected arguments appeared too. The case it
  was built for, premises and no conclusion, cannot occur there, because
  `ARG.concludes` is required and the lint already catches it. The owner's
  point settled it: what a record calls unfinished is a pattern it can
  write, so luria should not guess. Rendering such a pattern is [#373](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/373).
- A step held both by a field and by a pattern shows "through" only when it
  renders under that parent. CLAIM-027 rests on CLAIM-080 directly and
  through ARG-009, renders under another parent, and so shows no "through".
  Minor, and left alone.

## Pattern pages, and what nucleation said about them

*2026-10-13 07:51:54*

[#373](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/373) gives a named pattern a page of its matches ([ADR-132](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-132.md)), as a view
luria supplies on its own template, `luria:pattern.md.j2`.

`pattern_match/2`, a clingo-tuple reader in `logic` and

version pass with the same output, link targets included.

- **`match` returned one row per whole match**, so two matches differing
  only in an anonymous node were two identical rows. It now collapses them.
- **No pair of outputs was checked for collisions**; now all are, in one place.
- **YAML eats property maps**: fold (`>-`) or quote a pattern holding one.
- **`luria new changelog --name <branch>` returns an existing path** on a

On nucleation the unopposed count moved from 115 of 175 theses to 286 of

## Views as templates: fired on nucleation's CLAUDE.md

*2026-10-15 22:55:38*

Phase 1 of [ADR-130](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-130.md) is the `views` family: a Jinja template rendered
by `luria index`. Its context is `doc`, `docs`, `vocabulary`, `schemes` and
`journals`. Before trusting it ([DP-006](../../record/principles.d/DP-006.md)), I fired it on two real cases, each
in a scratch copy.

**nucleation's `CLAUDE.md`, as a template.** I stripped every hand-written
link back to its bare code, `ANTH-LIT-285` and the other remote codes
included, and replaced "Where things are" with a loop over `schemes()`. The
render matched the committed file byte for byte outside the templated
section: the fixer re-linked every code, local and remote, exactly as it had
been written by hand. Rendering took 0.4 s on nucleation's 3,100 documents.
The firing found two gaps, both now closed. `schemes()` lacked the scheme's
`title` and `blurb`, and the journal directories (`workbench.d`,
`curation.d`) could not be listed. That is what `journals()` is for.

**A broken template in luria's own record.** A view citing `ADR-999` failed
`luria lint` with exit 1 and the line
`views.x: record/views.d/x.md.j2:5: ADR-999 names no document in this record`.
With the line removed, the view rendered, `luria index --check` reported it
current, and the existing docs-index rule asked for its entry in
`docs/README.md`. A view under `docs/` is held to what any page there is.

**Traps found along the way:**

- `trim_blocks` eats the newline after `{% endfor %}`. That is Jinja's
  documented behaviour and the right default for markdown built from
  loops, but a one-line loop needs `join` or an explicit newline.
- The lint renders every view to find the broken ones, and at first it
  rendered each working one twice, once for the view tree and once for the
  check. `views.errors(rendered)` now re-renders only the views missing
  from the tree the lint already built.
- `test_a_generated_view_is_utf_8_whatever_the_console_is` runs luria in a
  subprocess with `HOME` replaced. A dependency installed only in the user
  site (`pip install --user`) is invisible there, so the test fails with
  `ModuleNotFoundError: jinja2` on a machine where everything else passes.
  CI installs the package properly and never hits this.

**`match()`, fired on nucleation's argument graph.** The inline pattern
`(c:CLAIM)<-[:concludes]-(g:ARG)-[:rests_on]->(p:CLAIM) WHERE NOT
(g {status: 'Rejected'})` and the declared `argued_from`, which is the same
pattern, return the same five rows. Among them is CLAIM-027 through ARG-009
from CLAIM-080, which is the claim's own `rests_on` in its frontmatter.
Without the `WHERE NOT` there are six. The sixth row goes through ARG-004,
which is Rejected, so the negation does its job. The first `match` in
a process took 7 s, nearly all of it building the record's facts. That is
the cost `luria index` already pays on nucleation for its pattern chains.
Each further pattern took about 0.3 s, one solve of `relations.lp` with the
pattern added.

The existing lowering could not serve a view as it stood. `pattern_edge`
gives a match's two ends and `pattern_via` its named inner nodes, each
keyed by the ends alone. Two matches sharing their ends but passing
through different inner nodes therefore cannot be told apart, and a row
cannot be rebuilt from them. `pattern_row` keys each named node by the
whole match instead, and is generated only when a view asks for it.

**Phase 3, fired on nucleation.** The template transcluded every claim on
the `will-organization` line. It read 28 claims: 14 Proposed, 11 Active,
2 Superseded and 1 Rejected. `retired-transclusions` reported the two
Superseded ones at line 6, the loop body: CLAIM-012 (by CLAIM-027) and
CLAIM-062 (by CLAIM-080). A separate read of CLAIM-012 at line 10, with
`inactive-ok:` on the line above, was excused. The site's "Rendered into"
for CLAIM-012 named `docs/probe.md`. The count is why retirement here is
`retires_on` and not the citation scan's "not Active": the scan's rule
would have reported 17 of the 28.

Siting a read needed no tracking of my own. Jinja compiles a template into
Python whose module globals hold `__jinja_template__`, and
`Template.get_corresponding_lineno` maps a compiled line back to the source
line. Walking up from the read to the first frame that carries one finds
the innermost template, an `include`d file included.

Phase 1 had a gap that this phase found. A view's output was not
`is_generated`, so the citation scan read the rendered `CLAUDE.md` and
would have reported a retired code there, in a file the next build
overwrites. Chain pages are excluded for the same reason, and view outputs
now are too.

**Phase 4, fired on nucleation through the CLI.** A pinned view quoted
ARG-003's "The inference" and named the claim it concludes.
`luria views --pin paper` endorsed two documents, ARG-003 and CLAIM-086.
I then reworded the quoted inference. `luria views` showed the view as
drifted, the lint row named ARG-003, and `luria index` left the published
sentence in `docs/paper.md` untouched. After re-endorsing, I reworded a
line under "Critical questions", which the paper does not quote, and
there was no drift. That second edit is the reason the lock hashes the
values each document was read for and not the document's file: hashing
the file would have reported it.

Naming trap: the CLI's flag is `--pin`, and Fire maps a flag to a
parameter of the same name. So the module function could not also be
called `pin` without the parameter shadowing it inside `run`. It is
`endorse`.

## CLAUDE.md derives its list of generated files

*2026-10-16 04:56:51*

`CLAUDE.md` named the generated files by hand, in a bullet saying never to
edit them. The list is now derived in its template, from loops over
`schemes()`, `journals()`, `chains()` and `views()`, plus `paths()` for
the pages luria renders at fixed places. A first version put the list in
`Config.generated()` and had `is_generated` ask it, so the check and the
page would share one list. It was dropped in review: the labels and the
loops are presentation and belong in the template, and `is_generated` was
right as it stood.

The cost is a second derivation of "what luria writes", in the template,
so the guard is a property and not a list ([DP-003](../../record/principles.d/DP-003.md)). Every file
`luria index` renders for this record has to fall under a path the
rendered bootloader names. I fired it once ([DP-006](../../record/principles.d/DP-006.md)): with the journals
loop deleted from the template, it failed and named
`docs/devlog/2026-10.md`. A new kind of generated output fails it until
the template learns to say it.

Trap: `adr_index.outputs()` includes nested records' views ([ADR-078](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-078.md)),
which this record's bootloader does not name. The test asks
`outputs(nested=False)`.

<a id="20261027034037"></a>

## A pull request's repair rebased in a newer push's unrepaired commits, and the lint read them

*2026-10-27 03:40:37*

Write the entry here: what problem was solved, what the fix was, and
what was found along the way — the failed approaches and the traps the
next person would otherwise rediscover.

**A downstream record kept seeing stale reds from the pull-request shape ([ADR-068](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-068.md)).** Nucleation adopted a working rule of pushing each commit to its pull request as it is made, with CI as the check. Twice in one day, nucleation#334 and [#338](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/338), a `docs-check` run went red on a commit that the next run passed. Every violation was a bare code or a missing converse, which is exactly what `luria repair` fixes.

The cause is in the generate action. The pull-request step commits the repair, then runs `git pull --rebase` so that the push lands on a branch that may have moved. When it has moved, the rebase brings the newer push's commits into this run's tree, unrepaired. The lint then runs in the same job, on that tree, and reports them. The newer push's own run repairs them a few minutes later, so the red is always stale. It still reads as a failure, and in a large record it costs a full run.

The fix repairs again when the rebase brought commits in. The step remembers the commit it checked out, and if that is no longer the parent of its repair commit after the rebase, it runs `luria repair` once more and commits the result before pushing. The lint then reads a tree in which every commit is repaired. The push can still race a third push, but that window is the seconds between the rebase and the push, not the length of a run.

A project can also cancel overtaken runs with a concurrency group, as nucleation now does. That saves the run and avoids the race, but only for a project whose workflow has the group, and the action is shared by every project, including one that wrote its own workflow. So both changes are made: the action repairs again after the rebase, and the template workflow `luria init` scaffolds, and this repository's own CI, now cancel a pull request's overtaken runs. The group is scoped to pull requests: every other run gets a group of its own, because a shared group drops a queued run even without `cancel-in-progress`, and runs on the default branch must serialize. Fired before trusting ([DP-006](../../record/principles.d/DP-006.md)): against a scratch remote with a stub `luria`, a newer push landing during the run left the old step pushing a tree with one of the two files unrepaired. The new step repaired both and pushed two repair commits.

## Pattern-backed warning classes, reliance and bounded acknowledgements

*2026-10-27 20:01:34*

**A downstream backlog luria never surfaced.** [Nucleation's forcing-functions decision](https://github.com/dmarx/nucleation/blob/main/record/decisions.d/ADR-057.md#forcing-functions-making-the-backlog-visible-to-the-lint) measured three blind spots behind more than a thousand undecided documents: credence across an edge was no finding (an Active claim resting on a Proposed one), nothing counted what rests on an undecided document, and an `inactive-ok-file` over a Superseded premise silenced the question forever. [ADR-131](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-131.md) makes each a lint finding a record turns on by configuration.

**One matcher.** A reported pattern's rows are a fourth shown predicate of the existing lowering, `pattern_node(P, Match, I, X)`, positional so that a match with no named node is still a row. `pattern_edge/3` was not enough: a single-node pattern emits none, and an all-anonymous one emits no `pattern_row/4`. The class list the dials check is now `lint.failable()` and `lint.mutable()`, which add the record's reported patterns to the static `FAILABLE` and `MUTABLE`. The tuples stay, because a dozen tests assert built-in classes against them.

**The YAML in the request did not parse.** `match: (c:CLAIM {status: 'Active'})-[...]` is a plain scalar containing `: `, which YAML refuses ("mapping values are not allowed here"). The first fixture failed on load before any luria code ran. A `match:` with a property map must be quoted, and the configuration reference's example now is.

**Reliance is `held/4` closed in clingo.** `logic/reliance.lp` takes `reliance(F)` facts as program text, so the memo key distinguishes configurations. Reading `held/4` rather than `ref_value` means a dependence stated only by the premise's converse field (`supports`) counts. The test fixture states one edge that way, and the count of 3 depends on it. A cycle does not make a document its own dependent.

**"Retired" for the expiry check is out of force and not undecided.** Luria's own `retired-citations` treats every non-Active target as retired, which would demand a date on every acknowledged citation of a draft. A `Proposed` premise is what `load-bearing` ranks instead, and a test pins that.

**Fired on fixtures ([DP-006](../../record/principles.d/DP-006.md)).** Each new class has a test that fires it on the shape it exists for and checks the row's text, beside a control that changes one thing and sees it go quiet: an `until` added, the field dropped from `reliance`, `reliance` unset, the target Proposed. The dials are fired too: `fail_on` failing on `inverted_premise` and `load-bearing`, `mute`, a `baseline` holding at 1 and then reporting 2 over it, and `fail_on` refusing a pattern the record has not declared `report: true`.

## Pattern pages as outlines, and the dialectic at fixed depth

*2026-10-28 02:20:16*

A pattern page now nests its matches as an outline, and patterns that share
an `output` merge into one ([ADR-133](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-133.md)). This answers the case PR [#380](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/380) was
written for, a claim, the argument concluding it and the claims undercutting
that argument, without changing chains.

**The step renderer moved before anything else changed.** `chains._link`,
`_annotation` and `_step` became `luria/steps.py`. A chain page captured
from `main` was pinned as a test first, and it passed before and after the
move. The one generalisation is that a facet the document's scheme cannot
hold is skipped. A chain refuses such a facet at load, so for a chain that
check never fires; for a pattern it is what lets `role` show on claims and
not on arguments.

**The tree is a sort, not a walk.** Every prefix of every match goes into
one dict keyed by its codes, and sorting the keys gives preorder: a prefix
sorts before its extensions, and siblings sort by code. Equal code tuples
are the same node, so a short pattern that is a prefix of a longer one adds
nothing twice. That is merging by position, because the key is the
position's code, not the pattern's variable name.

**One view per output.** `_check_rendered` keys by path, and `_RENDERED`
and `views.outputs()` key by output too, so two pattern views on one path
would have been last-wins. The patterns sharing a page now become one
`View`, keyed `patterns.<first>`, whose `where` names all of them. The
collision check needed one change: it names a pattern page by its first
pattern's key (`luria.yaml: patterns.bare: …`), not by the joined `where`.

**Holding a facet is decided in the logic core**, beside the chain's rule:
`pat_facet/2`, `pat_shown/2` (the label of each named node) and
`pattern_facet_unheld/2` in `consistency.lp`. The wording copies the
chain's, with "neither CLAIM nor ARG declares" for two schemes.

**Nucleation** (scratch copy, `lint.network: never`): without a pattern
`output`, index and lint output are identical to `main`. With the
bare/undercut pair the outline has 9 conclusions, 11 argument nodes over 10
ARGs (ARG-001 concludes CLAIM-057 and CLAIM-086, so it is drawn under both)
and 9 undercutters. An independent script over the frontmatter, reading
`undercuts` and `undercut_by` from both sides, found the same 11 pairs and 9
triples. The four ARGs nothing undercuts are on the page with nothing under
them. The only new lint finding was the docs-index entry for the page.

**Traps.** A template's error line moves whenever the template does. The
render-error test now covers both layouts with their own lines (33 and 13).
In the example, a bare code in the README needs `luria link --fix` run
under `LURIA_ROOT=examples/argument-map`. Run from the repository root, it
reads the root's schemes and leaves `OBJ-001` alone.

## Lint on a 5,500-file record spent four minutes on one regex, and the thread pool hid where the rest went

*2026-10-28 08:27:06*

**`luria lint` took about ten minutes on dmarx/nucleation.** Timed with the network off (`lint.network: never`, so upstream answers cannot vary the output), it was 614s on 5,519 scanned files. It is now 145s, and the lint's output is byte-identical to `main`'s.

**The profile to take is a serial one.** `py-spy record --idle --threads` on the pooled run said the chain pages took 86s and that `facts.fingerprint` took 52s of that. Run alone, the chain pages took 5s and the fingerprint under half a second over 13 calls. The rest was waiting for the interpreter lock. Almost everything in lint is CPU-bound Python, so the render pool overlaps nothing: `LURIA_JOBS=1` took 146s and the default width 150s. A pooled profile attributes lock waits to whatever frame was waiting, so it accuses the wrong code. `LURIA_JOBS=1 python -m cProfile` gives an honest one, as `parallel.py` says.

**The wrong first theory was the logic core.** The owner suspected the record's facts were rebuilt on every ask. They are not. `facts()` is memoized, and a lint builds them twice (about 36,000 and 42,000 facts, about 2s each). Every `derive()` call re-stats every document to prove nothing changed, but that costs under 0.1s a call when nothing else is running. The whole logic path, facts and solves together, was about a tenth of the run once the larger costs were gone. Caching facts across runs would save seconds, not minutes.

**Most of the time was one regex.** `bibliography._LEAD_RE` reads an author-year lead. Its name pattern and its joiner overlap: `A.` is both a surname and an initial, and a run of commas and spaces splits several ways. Its run of names is capped at 40. A 26-author entry, `LIT-1357`'s, has more than 50 name tokens, so the match must fail, and the engine tries every split first. That block alone took 254s, and `re` holds the interpreter lock while it matches, so every other thread stalled too. That is why the solves showed 23s of wall time against 2s of CPU. Making the run possessive (`{0,40}+`, Python 3.11+) commits to the longest run of names, and a failing lead fails in linear time. Against 342,529 blocks in nucleation and luria, old and new leads differ on two. Both are `F2013 and F2016`, which the old pattern read as `F2013 and F`, published in 2016, by giving back the digits of a name. `is_entry` gives the same answer for both.

**The rest was per-character Python and repeated work:**

- `doc_refs.masked` and `find_refs` set flags one character at a time, and `_line_index` walked every character to find newlines. Slices and `bisect` do the same in C.
- `find_refs`, `legacy_spellings` and `ref_status._scan` ran two regexes per scheme over every file, about 77 passes on nucleation. A leading `\b` stops `re` from searching for the literal prefix first, so each pass cost the same whether or not the prefix was there. A substring test now skips a scheme whose prefix is absent. It is exact only for a prefix with no regex metacharacters, so it is applied only then.
- `ref_status._scan` ran those passes once per line. Codes never span a line break, so it now matches the whole text and files each code by line, with the line breaks `str.splitlines` uses. A test pins that a form feed and U+2028 count as `splitlines` counts them. It passes on `main` as well.
- `contract.resolvable` rebuilt a scheme's whole code set for each of 38,000 asks: 26 million `Scheme.code` calls. It is now held against the identity of the scheme's cached listing, so a new listing is a miss.
- `is_generated`, `is_historical` and `link_base` compared each path against every view, vocabulary directory and journal on every call, through pathlib's slow `__eq__`. They now index the config once, in `cached_property`s on `Config`, which is never mutated after it is built.
- `lint.status_sections` called `ref_status.scan(docs=docs)`, which bypasses the corpus-scan cache. So every lint scanned the corpus twice. `reports.reference_status` had the same bug fixed before, and that comment says why.

**Not done, and where the remaining time goes.** Of the 145s, the reference report's corpus scan, the bare-reference scan and the annotation survey each read every file and build their own masks. `load_scheme` constructs about 107,000 `Adr` objects in a run, each with a deep copy of its frontmatter, because readings are per-object on purpose ([#233](https://github.com/dmarx/luria/issues/233)). Caching a whole scheme's load across a run would be a design change, not a refactor. If changes stay localized, the next large step is per-file results cached across runs, keyed on a file's content and the config. A fact cache alone would not be it.
